text:
Morgan Blake: Dropping a compact mock for a mini-toolbar on the latency card — Figma: https://www.figma.com/file/mini-toolbar/latency-compact. The goal: quick percentiles, a density slider, and a tiny throughput sparkline without expanding the header.
Jules Park: Love the idea. Main concern: keyboard focus — the scrubber overlay currently traps focus so the mini-toolbar controls are unreachable by tab when the scrubber is active.
Ava Kim: can you repro steps?
Jules Park: 1) Tab to card header, 2) Enter scrubber -> scrubber overlay appears, 3) Press TAB, focus stays inside scrubber; can't reach the density slider or percentiles toggle. Expected linear order: scrubber -> mini-toolbar -> apply button.
Morgan Blake: hmm. Two approaches: 1) keep mini-toolbar outside scrubber overlay DOM so it's tabbable, 2) add a keyboard shortcut to toggle mini-toolbar focus. Thoughts?
Diego Ramos: prefer keeping it in DOM order — simpler for SRs. Also add an explicit aria-label on the toolbar container: "Mini toolbar: percentiles, density slider, throughput sparkline" so screen readers get context.
Ava Kim: microcopy question — what label for the slider? We've tried "Sampling fidelity", "Sample density", "Sampling granularity" in other threads. For this compact control I propose "Density slider" with ticks: Auto | 20% | 50% | 100% and tiny helper text: "Auto adjusts sampling to balance accuracy & cost."
Jules Park: "Density slider" reads clearly in the compact UI. It also maps well to the visual slider affordance. Make Auto the default and mark as "recommended" in the tooltip.
Morgan Blake: heatmap rendering note: at low density users keep reading holes as missing traffic. Proposal: draw a light stipple over buckets where density < 25% and add a small legend chip: "Stippled = low sample density; results may be noisy." Link to docs: https://docs.redwood.ai/observability/sampling
Diego Ramos: agree. Also soften bucket edges with a 1px blur so pixels don't look like holes. For accessibility, expose the legend with an id and add aria-describedby to the heatmap element.
Ava Kim: keyboard UX detail: implement a focused skip for scrubber to mini-toolbar: pressing Shift+Tab from scrubber goes to last toolbar control; tabbing forward goes into mini-toolbar as normal. Avoid adding extra global shortcuts.
Diego Ramos: small CSS pattern for DOM-order approach (semantic-first):

.p64-mini-toolbar { display:inline-flex; gap:8px; align-items:center; }
.p64-mini-toolbar [role="slider"] { width:110px; }
/* keep aria-labels on each control, no visually-hidden hacks */

A11y Bot: Snapshot saved for 1746001111 (mini-toolbar-density-ux). Lint: ensure toolbar container has aria-label and each control exposes its value (aria-valuenow for slider), legend id is present and referenced by heatmap aria-describedby.
Morgan Blake: Decision recap: 1) Mini-toolbar stays in DOM order before scrubber overlay so it's tabbable; 2) Label the container with aria-label "Mini toolbar: percentiles, density slider, throughput sparkline"; 3) Use "Density slider" with Auto (recommended) | 20% | 50% | 100% ticks; helper text "Auto adjusts sampling to balance accuracy & cost"; 4) Heatmap: stipple overlay for density <25% + 1px blur; legend chip exposed to SRs via aria-describedby; 5) Small keyboard tweak: Shift+Tab from scrubber goes to last toolbar control to avoid trap; file ticket UX-74321: https://redwood.atlassian.net/browse/UX-74321. I'll update the Figma and hand off to Eng tomorrow AM. :sparkles:
